nameStory: This mustard gets its name from the Isle of Man, a small island between England and Ireland where it was first scientifically described. The plant was discovered growing along the rocky coastlines of this windswept island, thriving in the harsh maritime conditions that would challenge most other plants.
description: Isle of Man Cabbage is a hardy member of the mustard family that looks somewhat like a wild cabbage or large mustard plant. It typically grows 1-3 feet tall with thick, somewhat fleshy leaves that help it survive in harsh coastal conditions. The plant produces clusters of four-petaled yellow flowers typical of the mustard family, followed by narrow seed pods. It's extremely rare in New England, with only a couple of documented sightings.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers with four petals arranged in a cross pattern, clustered at the top of stems. Each flower is about half an inch across and has a slightly sweet, honey-like fragrance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, somewhat succulent leaves that feel waxy to the touch. Lower leaves are deeply lobed like a dandelion, while upper leaves are smaller and may clasp the stem.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Narrow, elongated seed pods (called siliques) that split open when ripe to release small round seeds. Pods are typically 1-2 inches long and held upright.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as an upright plant with multiple branching stems from the base. Has a somewhat bushy appearance and can spread to form small colonies.

habitat: In its native range, this plant thrives in coastal areas with sandy or rocky soil, often right along shorelines where salt spray is common. The few New England sightings have been in disturbed coastal areas, possibly near ports where seeds might have arrived accidentally. It prefers full sun and well-drained soils.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges early, with the characteristic thick, waxy leaves forming a low rosette before the flowering stems develop.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with bright yellow flower clusters. This is the best time for identification when the distinctive four-petaled mustard flowers are most visible.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods mature and split open, releasing seeds. Leaves may persist and remain green well into autumn due to their succulent nature.
seasonality.winter: In mild coastal areas, some leaves may persist as a low rosette, though the plant typically dies back to the roots in harsh New England winters.

funFact: This tough little plant can actually tolerate salt water splashing on its leaves - a rare ability that allows it to grow right at the ocean's edge where most plants would quickly die from salt poisoning.
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other yellow-flowered mustards like Winter Cress or Wild Radish, but the thick, waxy leaves and coastal habitat help distinguish it. The succulent-like feel of the leaves is a dead giveaway - most other mustards have thin, papery leaves.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name suggesting it's a type of cabbage, this plant is only distantly related to true cabbage. Like many mustard family members, the 'cabbage' name comes from the general similarity of the leaves, though Isle of Man Cabbage is much smaller and more specialized for harsh coastal conditions.
compareHints: Isle of Man Cabbage is the only species in its genus found in North America, making it unique among New England mustards. Compared to other coastal mustards like Sea Rocket, it has more deeply divided lower leaves and a more upright growth habit rather than sprawling along the ground.
